chapter.title: Beyond the standard: dialects and experimental Lojban

section.title: What this chapter is, and is not
section.para:
experimental cmavodefined
dialectsof Lojban
The main reference chapters of this book teach the account of Lojban that this edition selected. Where they teach a rule, they give its status: ratified, committee-approved, checkpointed, de facto, or unsettled. This chapter describes something else. It describes words and grammatical variants that no official body ever adopted. But a reader of real Lojban text will meet them sooner or later.

We call a single unadopted word an experimental cmavo, and a coherent set of unadopted grammar changes a dialect. Nothing in this chapter is official, and you do not need any of it to speak or read standard Lojban. But a reference that ignores these things does not describe the language as people use it.

experimental cmavoword-forms reserved for
Standard Lojban itself provides the space where these words live.
explains that the language reserves the cmavo shapes beyond the simple assigned forms (such as the longer vowel strings in zo'oi or su'oi) for experimental use. They are grammatical word forms with no officially assigned meaning. Coining one breaks no rule, and the new word has whatever standing its users give it. The community dictionaries record such words, clearly marked as unofficial. Deliberate change to the official language stopped (see ), so this decentralized process is now the source of all new function words.

dotsideas dialect that became official
The boundary between experimental and adopted moved in the past too. This book writes every cmevla with a dot at the start and at the end. That rule began as a deliberately partisan dialect, and its name, the dot side, was a joke. It is now committee-approved (see
for the details).

The established corpus itself grew from once-experimental proposals, adopted at various levels. The difference now is that the bodies that had the power to promote such proposals no longer meet. In that sense, the features in this chapter are proposals with no one left to propose them to. Their standing rises and falls with usage alone.

parsersdialect support in
A feature needs two things to earn a place in this chapter, and each section states both. The first is usage evidence: the feature appears in genuine text or in established community writing, not only in a dictionary entry. The second is machine support: at least one maintained parser accepts it. The parsers matter because the community actually uses them to delimit its dialects.

The standard camxes grammar accepts only standard Lojban. Its beta variant adds the popular experimental cmavo that are backward-compatible. Further variants add the genuine grammar changes at the end of this chapter. Other tools take the opposite approach: they accept the popular experimental cmavo by default, and they keep explicit dialect switches for the true grammar changes. We made sure that at least one such parser accepts every example in this chapter, and each section says which.

experimental cmavostatus of
All of these features are unofficial. None is ratified, committee-approved, or checkpointed. Where a section cites usage frequency, the evidence is a community survey of six corpora from 2015. Its counts give too much weight to chat logs and to individual authors. Treat it as a rough rank order, not as an endorsement.

section.title: Quoting the outside world: zo'oi and friends
section.para: This section discusses the following experimental cmavo. (In the cmavo lists of this chapter, a star on a selma'o name marks an unofficial assignment. This is either an experimental selma'o, like ZOhOI*, or an experimental addition to a standard selma'o, like PA* later on.)

cmavo-entry.description: quote next word as a rafsi

section.para: zo'oi Standard Lojban quotes non-Lojban material with zoi ... . This requires a delimiting word, said twice (see ). For a single foreign word, that ceremony is heavy, and some of the best-attested experimental cmavo shorten it. The word zo'oi quotes exactly one following word, just as zo does for a single Lojban word. In speech, pauses delimit the quoted word. In writing, whitespace (spaces, tabs, or line breaks) delimits it:

la'oi Its sibling la'oi does the same for names. It stands to la'o as zo'oi stands to zoi. In the community's 2015 frequency survey, it ranked first among all experimental cmavo. That is no surprise, because foreign names of one word (of people, software, and websites) are everywhere:

me'oi ra'oi Two rarer members complete the family. The word me'oi makes an ad-hoc predicate out of a foreign word. The community calls the result a stage-0 fu'ivla: a borrowing that skips even the minimal Lojbanization of :
and ra'oi quotes a single word as a rafsi. This is useful because many rafsi are not words at all, so zo cannot quote them:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: ra'oi bra cu rafsi zo barda
interlinear-gloss.natlang: The rafsi bra belongs to barda.

section.para: Genuine text attests all four: la'oi and zo'oi heavily, and me'oi and ra'oi more thinly. The standard camxes grammar rejects all four. The camxes beta family accepts them, and so does jbotci, without any dialect switch.

section.title: Plural quantifiers: su'oi and ro'oi
section.para: This section discusses the following experimental cmavo:

plural quantification su'oi ro'oi The official quantifiers su'o and ro are singular. A variable that they bind stands for one individual at a time (see ). That leaves a genuine gap. Some predicates are true of several things taken together, but not of any one of them. Examples are gather, surround, and be a twosome. You cannot build a claim like some people are gathering from a singular quantifier at all, because no single person gathers.
Standard Lojban fills the gap with constants. An unquantified lo prenu can refer to people jointly, and loi forms groups. But standard Lojban has no way to quantify plurally.
The experimental pair su'oi and ro'oi supplies exactly that. A variable that they bind can stand for one or more things at once. With them, you can say:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: su'oi da poi prenu cu jmaji

section.para: where the da stands for the gatherers jointly. You can define each member of the pair from the other by the usual duality: su'oi da is na ku ro'oi da na ku. This exactly parallels the singular rules of .

The standard camxes grammar rejects these quantifiers. The camxes beta family and jbotci accept them. The rigorous writing that uses them is the work of a small circle of theorists, not everyday text. The logic chapters of this book use only the official singular quantifiers.

section.title: Other experimental cmavo in real use
section.para:
error correctionexperimental quote set
lo'ai sa'ai le'ai Beyond the quotation family, the community's frequency surveys put one coherent set clearly ahead of the rest. This set is the error-correction quotes lo'ai, sa'ai, and le'ai. The erasure words of standard Lojban (see ) can only erase the most recent words. But in live conversation, people often want to reach back and repair something that they said a sentence ago. The set works like a search-and-replace: lo'ai quotes the wrong text, sa'ai quotes its replacement, and le'ai closes the correction:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi klama lo zarci .i lo'ai zarci sa'ai zdani le'ai
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I go-to a market. [wrong:] market [replace-with:] house [correction-end]
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I went to the market – I mean, the house.

section.para: xo'e Two single words also came into real use. The word xo'e is the elliptical digit. It is to numbers what zo'e is to sumti: an unspecified quantity that the speaker chooses not to give:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Some number of people are coming.

section.para: zo'ei The word zo'ei (with a grammar like LAhE) means something associated with ..., roughly zo'e pe. It often takes the place of a tu'a that a lazy speaker stretches beyond its abstraction sense. For example, mi viska zo'ei la .paris. means I see something related to Paris: a photograph, perhaps, or the skyline.

A caveat on support: no camxes grammar recognizes zo'ei as a word, because in camxes the string collides with a zo quotation. The danger is silent. A full sentence like the one above still parses in camxes, as a quotation of 'ei, with an entirely different structure. jbotci recognizes zo'ei properly.
Several more words circulate, with thinner but real use. This book records them only by name:

listitem.para: The selma'o quoter ma'oi (ma'oi ba names selma'o PU by example)
The abstractor poi'i, common in the plural-logic literature of

section.para: The camxes beta family and jbotci accept the error-correction set and xo'e. Only jbotci accepts zo'ei. The camxes beta family accepts the words that this section only names, but jbotci's support for them varies from word to word. Make sure that your parser accepts a word before you rely on it. None of these words is official.

section.title: The cmevla-brivla merger
section.para: cmevla-brivla merger The dialects so far add words. The remaining two change grammar. The cmevla-brivla merger (CBM) removes the grammatical wall between name words and predicate words. Under it, a cmevla like .djan. can serve as a selbri or a tanru unit. It then predicates of its subject, and the users of the dialect decide its precise place structure. Also, the article la becomes an ordinary descriptor that takes whatever selbri follows.

The motivating complaint is pedagogical. In standard Lojban, la behaves one way before a cmevla and another way before a brivla. Learners who discover that predicates can name things are tempted to write what the standard grammar forbids. Standard camxes and the default grammar of jbotci reject the following sentence, but under CBM it is fine:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: This John-s, so to speak. (CBM dialect only)

section.para: The merger reinterprets existing forms, and does not only add new ones. So it is not backward-compatible: the same string of standard Lojban can parse differently under CBM. The two tested implementations are the camxes cbm grammars and the cbm dialect switch of jbotci. They do not agree in every corner about how aggressively to reinterpret la phrases. But they agree on the new permission itself: a cmevla can predicate.

CBM is a real dialect, parsers implement it, and it has an established design literature. But people discuss it more than they write it: running text wholly in CBM is scarce. In the tested tools, it requires an explicit dialect grammar or switch.

section.title: Short words for common meanings: ce-ki-tau-jau
section.para: ce-ki-tau-jau The last dialect is a family of cmavo swaps, with the label ce-ki-tau-jau. The dialect starts from this diagnosis. Some of the busiest cmavo of the language have two syllables: ce'u, ke'a, tu'a, jo'u, and du'u. But some one-syllable forms are nearly idle: ce, ki, tau, jau, and du.

The dialect swaps each pair. In ce-ki-tau-jau text, ce means what ce'u means in this book, and the reverse. In principle, each swap works in both directions, and speakers can adopt each one separately. (In practice, as the community's own record notes, the swaps mostly run one way. The short forms get the busy meanings as synonyms, and the long forms also keep their old senses.)

The trap is that most of the short forms also have meanings in standard Lojban. So a swapped sentence often parses in both grammars, with different meanings. For example, lo broda poi ki broda is a sticky-tense construction to a standard parser, and a relative clause with ke'a to a ce-ki-tau parser. So text in this dialect is unintelligible to a standard reader in a peculiarly silent way. Nothing fails, but the text means something else. Well-behaved text in the dialect announces itself first, with a header like jo'au tcekitaujau (the community convention).

Neither tested implementation matches the primary proposal of five pairs exactly. The camxes ckt grammar implements the ce / ki / tau / du swaps and several others, but not jau. The ce-ki-tau-jau dialect of jbotci implements ce / ki / tau / jau, adds a su'o-to-su swap, and omits du. It also prints back the standard equivalents.
By the community's own assessment, people use the dialect very little. This book includes it as the clearest worked example of what a dialect is. The text of this book uses none of the swaps.
